partners.diseaseBName: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome due to CREBBP mutations
partners.mechanism_chain: RAI1 (HGNC:9796) —DISRUPTS→ gene transcription regulation (GO:0006351); CREBBP (HGNC:2603) —DISRUPTS→ histone acetylation (GO:0016573); histone acetylation (GO:0016573) —BINDS→ gene transcription regulation (GO:0006351); gene transcription regulation (GO:0006351) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); gene transcription regulation (GO:0006351) —LEADS_TO→ Global developmental delay (HP:0001263); gene transcription regulation (GO:0006351) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal facial shape (HP:0000274). Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 (Smith-Magenis syndrome) and loss-of-function mutations in CREBBP (Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome) both converge on the dysregulation of gene transcription. CREBBP is a critical component of the transcriptional machinery, primarily through its histone acetyltransferase activity, which is essential for proper gene expression. RAI1 also plays a role in transcriptional regulation, although its precise mechanisms are less understood. The disruption of these key regulators leads to widespread transcriptional abnormalities, ultimately manifesting as shared phenotypic features such as intellectual disability, developmental delay, and abnormal facial features.

**Proposed mechanism:** RAI1 (HGNC:9828) —DISRUPTS→ Neuronal development and function (GO:0048666); Neuronal development and function (GO:0048666) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); HBB (HGNC:4827) —DISRUPTS→ Hematopoietic stem cell differentiation (GO:0007255); Hematopoietic stem cell differentiation (GO:0007255) —LEADS_TO→ Erythrocytosis (HP:0001900); Neuronal development and function (GO:0048666) —INCREASES→ Hematopoietic stem cell differentiation (GO:0007255). Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 disrupts normal neuronal development and function, leading to intellectual disability characteristic of Smith-Magenis syndrome. Concurrently, loss-of-function mutations in HBB impair hemoglobin production or stability, affecting erythropoiesis and leading to erythrocytosis. The proposed convergence is that impaired neuronal function (n6) can indirectly influence hematopoietic stem cell differentiation (n5), potentially exacerbating or modulating the erythrocytosis phenotype, or vice versa, where altered hematopoiesis impacts oxygen delivery to the brain, affecting neuronal function.

**How to falsify it:** Absence of any discernible interaction or cross-talk between the downstream pathways of RAI1 and HBB in relevant cellular models (e.g., induced pluripotent stem cells derived from patients) would falsify this hypothesis. Furthermore, if genetic studies show no correlation between the severity of neurological symptoms and erythrocytosis in patients with compound heterozygous or biallelic mutations in both genes, this would weaken the proposed link. _(variant: Presence of common variants in RAI1 or HBB in the general population (gnomAD frequency > 1%) that do not segregate with either disease would challenge the causal link for those specific variants.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding this potential mechanistic link could reveal novel therapeutic targets for managing overlapping symptoms or co-occurring conditions in patients with Smith-Magenis syndrome and familial erythrocytosis. It might also shed light on the complex interplay between neurological and hematological systems.
